transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I barely sleep right anymore. I'll just lie there in bed hearing rain or thinking about the bluff giving way. It's like my brain won't turn off. And you know, it's funny, my bed is actually really comfortable. I got this memory foam mattress topper a few months ago on sale at Target. It was supposed to help my back because sitting at the call center all day really does a number on your posture. They don't give us good chairs, just these cheap plastic ones that squeak every time you lean back. My buddy Dave, he works there too, he actually brought in his own cushion, but management told him he couldn't use it because it wasn't "standard issue." Can you believe that? Anyway, when I do finally pass out, I just wake up sweaty from these dreams. Then I have to show up to the call center feeling like I never slept at all.
You mentioned having dreams that leave you sweaty, are these dreams scary or disturbing?

Yeah, they're... they're pretty bad. It's not just the dreams, though. Even when I'm awake, stuff pops in my head out of nowhere. Like, I'll just be sitting there, and suddenly I hear the sound of rocks sliding, or I feel my leg stuck under me again. For a minute, I'm right back on that trail instead of sitting at my desk with a headset on. It's wild because our headsets at work are the absolute worst. The mic barely picks up anything unless you basically eat it, and the earpiece gets so hot after a couple of hours. I asked my supervisor, Linda, if we could get new ones, and she just gave me this look, like I was asking for a gold-plated chair. Linda's always stressed, though. I think her kid is going through some stuff at school, which, you know, I get it, kids are tough. But man, when that sound hits me, the rocks... it just takes over everything.
Did something specific happen that started these dreams and thoughts about the bluff and the trail?

Yeah, it was about four months ago. The trail up on the bluff collapsed while I was out there, and I got trapped under all this dirt and rock. I was actually wearing these brand new boots I ordered online when it happened. Man, the shipping on those was a total joke. They said two-day delivery, but it took almost two weeks. I kept checking the tracking on my phone, and it just sat at the warehouse in the next town over forever. My buddy Dave—the guy from the call center I was telling you about—he told me to just cancel the order and get a refund, but I really wanted them for that hike. They were this really nice waterproof suede stuff. Completely ruined them, obviously, when the ground gave way and pinned me. But yeah... it's been going on for four months, ever since I got stuck out there.
Do these thoughts and dreams happen more often when you're reminded of the trail or the bluff, like when you see something that looks like it or talk to someone who was there?

Well, I guess I wouldn't really know about talking to the people who were there or going back, because I just... I completely avoid it. Like, I won't even go near the coast trails anymore. And my hiking buddies, they keep texting me to hang out or go on easy walks, and I just dodge their messages. Even just the thought of talking about going out there makes my chest tighten up. 

It's actually kind of annoying because my phone is constantly buzzing with their group chat. I got this new phone plan a while ago, unlimited data, which is great, but the coverage is spotty at best. I'll be in the breakroom at the call center, trying to watch a video or something on my lunch, and I get zero bars. Linda, my supervisor, she has the same carrier and swears by it, but she also has the newest iPhone, so maybe that's why. I'm still using this clunker from three years ago. The screen has a crack right across the middle from when I dropped it getting out of my car. I tried putting one of those screen protectors on it, but it bubbled up all weird in the corner. Anyway, yeah, I just ignore their texts. I can't deal with it.
Do you think these thoughts and dreams would happen if you weren't reminded of the trail or the bluff at all?

I don't know, honestly. I mean, they just kind of happen. Even when I'm just sitting at my desk, like I said, and I'm not even thinking about hiking or the outdoors at all. I'll just be staring at my monitor. We use this ancient software at work, it's seriously from like the early 2000s or something. The interface is all gray and blocky, and it crashes if you try to open more than three customer accounts at once. Dave figured out this trick where if you hit refresh right as it freezes, sometimes it un-sticks itself, but usually you just have to reboot the whole computer. And the computers take like ten minutes to start up. Linda hates it when we have to reboot because it messes up her call time metrics. But yeah, the thoughts just pop up whenever, even when I'm just looking at that stupid gray screen.
Are there any specific activities or places that you avoid because they remind you of the trail collapse?

Well, I mean, I already told you I don't go near the coast trails or talk to my hiking buddies. But other than that... I don't really know. I don't think there's anything else specific. I mostly just go to work and come home. 

Speaking of coming home, the commute has been absolutely brutal lately. They're doing this massive construction project on the highway, supposedly adding an HOV lane or something, but it's been going on for like six months and I swear they haven't actually done anything except put up a million orange cones. It backs traffic up for miles. Yesterday, I was stuck behind this guy in a pickup truck who had a bunch of unsecured scrap metal in the back, and every time we hit a bump, I thought a piece of pipe was going to fly through my windshield. I really need to get my brakes checked, too. They've been squeaking every time I stop, which makes sitting in bumper-to-bumper traffic even more miserable. Dave said he knows a guy who can do it cheap, but you know how that goes. Sometimes cheap just means you end up paying twice. But yeah, no, I don't really avoid anything else besides the trails.
Do you often feel guilty about what happened on the trail?

Yeah, I mean... I do. I just keep thinking about how stupid and careless I was for being out there alone in the first place. Like, I should have known better, right? And now it just feels like... like if I let my guard down anywhere, something bad is going to happen. It's exhausting. 

Kind of like how exhausted I am from trying to get my landlord to fix the AC in my apartment. I've been calling him for two weeks straight. It's just a window unit, but it rattles so loud you can't even hear the TV. I tried wedging a piece of cardboard in the side to stop the shaking, but it just blew out. And it's getting so hot in there, especially in the afternoons because my window faces west. The blinds are broken too, missing like three slats right in the middle, so the sun just bakes the whole room. I bought a cheap box fan from the dollar store, but it just pushes the hot air around. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has central air, and she's always bragging about how cool her place is. She's nice, but she talks way too much when I'm just trying to get my mail. But yeah, I just feel like I can't relax anywhere anymore because if I do, I'll mess up again.
Do you avoid talking or thinking about your feelings related to the trail collapse?

Well, I mean, I try not to think about it. Like I said before, I won't go near the coast trails at all anymore. And I've been dodging texts from my hiking buddies, too. Just... even thinking about talking to them about going out there, or talking about how I feel about it, my chest just gets so tight I can't breathe right. 

It's actually kind of like how my chest felt when I was trying to move this old couch out of my apartment last weekend. I bought this new one off Craigslist—well, it's not new, it's used, but it's new to me. It's this dark brown leather, or maybe faux leather, I don't know, but it looks nice. Anyway, the guy who sold it to me said he'd help me carry it up the stairs, but he just dropped it at the bottom and drove off. So I had to drag the old one down and the new one up all by myself. My buddy Dave was supposed to help, but he bailed at the last minute because his car wouldn't start. He drives this beat-up Honda Civic that's always breaking down. I keep telling him he needs to just trade it in, but he's attached to it for some reason. But yeah, dragging that couch up three flights of stairs... I thought my heart was going to explode, my chest was so tight. So yeah, I just avoid talking about the trail stuff because I don't want to feel like that.
Do you try to avoid feeling the emotions that come up when you think about the trail collapse?

Yeah, I mean... I do. Like I was saying, I won't go near the coast trails at all now, and I just dodge all the texts from my hiking buddies. Even just talking about going out there or thinking about it makes my chest tighten up so bad. It's just easier to push it all down, you know? 

Speaking of pushing things down, I had to completely cram my trash can full this morning. The garbage truck just drove right past my building yesterday. I don't know if they got a new driver or what, but they missed the whole block. So now everyone's bins are overflowing, and the seagulls are having an absolute field day. There's this one huge seagull that always sits on the streetlamp outside my window—I call him Captain Crunch because he sounds like he's crunching on rocks when he squawks. Anyway, he was ripping into this plastic bag of someone's takeout containers, just making a huge mess all over the sidewalk. The city is supposed to send someone to clean that stuff up, but they never do. You try calling the sanitation department and you just sit on hold listening to elevator music for forty-five minutes. But yeah, I just try not to feel any of that trail stuff, so I avoid anything that brings it up.
Do you try to push away memories or thoughts about the trail collapse when they come into your mind?

Yeah, I do. I mean, like I've been saying, I just try to push it all away. I won't go anywhere near those coast trails anymore, not even close. And when my hiking buddies text me, I just ignore them. I dodge them completely because if I even think about it, or try to talk about going out there, my chest just gets so tight I can't even breathe. It's just too much.

Which is funny because that's exactly how I felt when I was trying to fix my bike tire yesterday. I was pumping it up, and the valve just snapped right off. I don't even know how that happens. I bought the tube like two weeks ago from this guy at a swap meet. He said it was heavy-duty, but clearly he was lying. Now I have to walk to the bus stop, which is like six blocks away, and it's been raining off and on all week. Yesterday I got splashed by this massive puddle because some guy in a delivery truck was flying down the street. It was one of those white vans, you know, the ones that always look like they're in a rush? He didn't even slow down. Completely soaked my shoes. They're my work shoes, too, the ones with the non-slip soles because I work at the call center and they have these really slick linoleum floors in the breakroom. Last month, Brenda from accounting slipped and spilled her whole coffee. It was a mess. But yeah, if a memory about the trail pops up, I just try to shut it down immediately because of how bad it makes my chest feel.
Do you try to avoid thinking about the trail collapse when memories of it pop into your mind?

I feel like a broken record here, doc, but yeah. Just like I've been saying, I completely avoid the coast trails now. I won't go anywhere near them. And I'm still dodging all those texts from my hiking buddies because even just talking about going out there, or having it pop into my head, my chest gets so tight I can barely breathe. 

Dodging people is getting exhausting, though. It's kind of like how I have to dodge my supervisor at work. I do customer service, right? And they just brought in these new headsets for everyone on the floor. They're wireless, which sounds great, but the battery life is complete garbage. You'll be in the middle of talking to a customer about some billing issue, and the headset just beeps once and completely dies. Then the customer thinks you hung up on them, so they call back and they're just screaming at the next rep. My supervisor, Gary, keeps trying to pull me into these little one-on-one "coaching sessions" about my call drop rate, so I keep having to dodge him in the breakroom. Gary is one of those guys who wears a tie clip every single day even though we don't even have a dress code. It's this little silver golf club. I don't even think the guy plays golf, he just drinks those weird green smoothies that smell like grass. But yeah, if the trail stuff pops into my head, I just block it out immediately because I hate that tight feeling in my chest.
Do you find yourself avoiding thoughts, feelings, or memories related to the trail collapse?

Look, I don't know how many different ways I can say it. Yes. I avoid all of it. Like I told you, I stay completely away from the coast trails, and I just ignore my hiking buddies when they text me. Because if I even start thinking about it, or talking about going out there, my chest gets that horrible tight feeling.

Tight feelings are the worst. It's like when you wash a pair of jeans and put them in the dryer on high heat by mistake. I did that with my favorite pair of Levi's last weekend. I usually hang dry them over the shower rod, but my roommate's girlfriend was over and she took like a forty-five-minute shower, so the bathroom was basically a sauna. I didn't want my jeans smelling like her weird coconut shampoo, so I just threw them in the dryer. Big mistake. Now I can barely button them, and I have to wear them to work because my other pants got a bleach stain on the knee. We're not supposed to wear jeans at the call center anyway, but Gary hasn't said anything yet. Probably because he's too busy worrying about his golf club tie clip. But yeah, I avoid the thoughts and feelings and memories and all of it, just like I avoid the trails and the texts.
Have you noticed any significant impact on your daily life or relationships due to avoiding things that remind you of the trail collapse?

Yeah, I mean... it definitely has. My work has slipped a lot lately. I missed some important notes in the CRM system the other day, and a call ended up escalating to management. I actually got written up for it. Which really sucks because I was hoping to move up to team lead eventually, and now I'm worried I completely blew my chance. 

Getting written up is the worst feeling. It's on this bright pink paper, too. Like, they actually use pink paper for the disciplinary forms. It's so embarrassing. Gary handed it to me in a folder, but everyone knows what it means when you get called into his office and come out with a manila folder. It's like being back in high school when you get sent to the principal's office and have to carry that little slip down the hallway. I hated high school. That's why I dropped out, honestly. I've been trying to study for my GED, but I've completely fallen behind on that, too. I'm just so exhausted all the time. And like I said, I'm avoiding all the people I used to hike with, so I'm just sitting around doing nothing, too tired to even look at a textbook. The GED prep book I bought is massive, too. It's like three inches thick. I tried reading the math section last week, and it was just a bunch of fractions and word problems about trains leaving stations at different times. Who even takes trains anymore? Unless you live in a big city with a subway, I guess. But yeah, avoiding all the trail stuff and the people I hiked with is definitely messing up my work and my studying.
Do you often think that you're a bad person or that you're worthless because of what happened on the trail?

Well, I wouldn't say I think I'm a bad person, really, but... I do keep thinking I was just so stupid and careless for being out there alone in the first place. Like, I should have known better. And now it just feels like if I let my guard down anywhere, something bad is going to happen. 

Being alone out there is kind of like when I try to study for my GED by myself at the coffee shop down the street. It's this little independent place, not a Starbucks, and they have these terrible wobbly tables. I tried shoving a napkin under one of the legs the other day, but it was one of those really cheap, thin napkins that just sort of disintegrates when you fold it. The barista there is this guy with a huge handlebar mustache, which I feel like is such an outdated look, you know? He always spells my name wrong on the cup even though I'm literally the only person in there most afternoons. He wrote 'Carl' last time. My name doesn't even sound like Carl. But yeah, I just feel like I was really dumb for being on that trail by myself, and now I'm just waiting for the next bad thing to happen if I'm not careful.
Do you feel guilty about surviving the trail collapse when others might not have if they were in your situation?

Guilty? I don't know if guilt is the right word, but... I mean, most days I just feel scared and embarrassed right under the surface. Like everyone can tell I messed up out there and I'm not as tough as I used to act. 

Acting tough is so exhausting anyway. It's like my buddy Dave, he always acts like he's this huge tough guy because he drives a lifted truck. It's a Chevy Silverado, I think. Bright blue. He put these massive tires on it, and it's so high up you practically need a step stool to get in. I tore the seam on my good jacket trying to climb into the passenger seat once. It was this vintage windbreaker I found at a thrift store for like five bucks. The thrift store is right next to the bowling alley, which is weird because you always smell stale french fries when you're looking at the clothes. They have the best fries at that bowling alley, though. Crinkle cut. I don't know why, but crinkle cut just holds the ketchup better. But yeah, I just feel embarrassed all the time, like everyone knows I'm not actually tough at all.
Have you noticed any problems in your relationships or daily activities because of the thoughts, feelings, or memories related to the trail collapse?

Yeah, I mean... I think I already mentioned this, but it's definitely messing up my daily life. Like I said before, my work has slipped a lot. I missed those important notes in the CRM, the call escalated, and I got that pink write-up slip from Gary. Which really still bothers me because I wanted to be a team lead. And I'm just so exhausted all the time that I've completely fallen behind on studying for my GED. I'm just avoiding everyone I used to hike with, so I sit around doing nothing. 

Sitting around is actually really bad for your posture, you know? I read this article online about how sitting too much is the new smoking. It messes up your lower back. My dad had terrible lower back problems. He used to wear this weird brace thing under his shirt that looked like a corset. He bought it off some infomercial late at night. Those infomercials are wild, they always have people struggling in black and white to do basic things, like pouring milk, and then suddenly in color they have this miracle product. I bought a slap-chop thing once because of an infomercial. It actually worked pretty well for onions, but it was a nightmare to clean. The blades would get stuck. But yeah, the memories and stuff are definitely causing problems with my job and my studying.

I bought this new one off Craigslist—well, it's not new, it's used, but it's new to me. It's this dark brown leather, or maybe faux leather, I don't know, but it looks nice. Anyway, the guy who sold it to me said he'd help me carry it up the stairs, but he just dropped it at the bottom and drove off. So I had to drag the old one down and the new one up all by myself. My buddy Dave was supposed to help, but he bailed at the last minute because his car wouldn't start. He drives this beat-up Honda Civic that's always breaking down. I keep telling him he needs to just trade it in, but he's attached to it for some reason. But yeah, dragging that couch up three flights of stairs... I thought my heart was going to explode, my chest was so tight. So yeah, I just avoid talking about the trail stuff because I don't want to feel like that.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean... I do. Like I was saying, I won't go near the coast trails at all now, and I just dodge all the texts from my hiking buddies. Even just talking about going out there or thinking about it makes my chest tighten up so bad. It's just easier to push it all down, you know? 

Speaking of pushing things down, I had to completely cram my trash can full this morning. The garbage truck just drove right past my building yesterday. I don't know if they got a new driver or what, but they missed the whole block. So now everyone's bins are overflowing, and the seagulls are having an absolute field day. There's this one huge seagull that always sits on the streetlamp outside my window—I call him Captain Crunch because he sounds like he's crunching on rocks when he squawks. Anyway, he was ripping into this plastic bag of someone's takeout containers, just making a huge mess all over the sidewalk. The city is supposed to send someone to clean that stuff up, but they never do. You try calling the sanitation department and you just sit on hold listening to elevator music for forty-five minutes. But yeah, I just try not to feel any of that trail stuff, so I avoid anything that brings it up.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of avoidance of internal reminders
doctor.question: Do you try to push away memories or thoughts about the trail collapse when they come into your mind?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. I mean, like I've been saying, I just try to push it all away. I won't go anywhere near those coast trails anymore, not even close. And when my hiking buddies text me, I just ignore them. I dodge them completely because if I even think about it, or try to talk about going out there, my chest just gets so tight I can't even breathe. It's just too much.

Which is funny because that's exactly how I felt when I was trying to fix my bike tire yesterday. I was pumping it up, and the valve just snapped right off. I don't even know how that happens. I bought the tube like two weeks ago from this guy at a swap meet. He said it was heavy-duty, but clearly he was lying. Now I have to walk to the bus stop, which is like six blocks away, and it's been raining off and on all week. Yesterday I got splashed by this massive puddle because some guy in a delivery truck was flying down the street. It was one of those white vans, you know, the ones that always look like they're in a rush? He didn't even slow down. Completely soaked my shoes. They're my work shoes, too, the ones with the non-slip soles because I work at the call center and they have these really slick linoleum floors in the breakroom. Last month, Brenda from accounting slipped and spilled her whole coffee. It was a mess. But yeah, if a memory about the trail pops up, I just try to shut it down immediately because of how bad it makes my chest feel.

And I'm still dodging all those texts from my hiking buddies because even just talking about going out there, or having it pop into my head, my chest gets so tight I can barely breathe. 

Dodging people is getting exhausting, though. It's kind of like how I have to dodge my supervisor at work. I do customer service, right? And they just brought in these new headsets for everyone on the floor. They're wireless, which sounds great, but the battery life is complete garbage. You'll be in the middle of talking to a customer about some billing issue, and the headset just beeps once and completely dies. Then the customer thinks you hung up on them, so they call back and they're just screaming at the next rep. My supervisor, Gary, keeps trying to pull me into these little one-on-one "coaching sessions" about my call drop rate, so I keep having to dodge him in the breakroom. Gary is one of those guys who wears a tie clip every single day even though we don't even have a dress code. It's this little silver golf club. I don't even think the guy plays golf, he just drinks those weird green smoothies that smell like grass. But yeah, if the trail stuff pops into my head, I just block it out immediately because I hate that tight feeling in my chest.

Because if I even start thinking about it, or talking about going out there, my chest gets that horrible tight feeling.

Tight feelings are the worst. It's like when you wash a pair of jeans and put them in the dryer on high heat by mistake. I did that with my favorite pair of Levi's last weekend. I usually hang dry them over the shower rod, but my roommate's girlfriend was over and she took like a forty-five-minute shower, so the bathroom was basically a sauna. I didn't want my jeans smelling like her weird coconut shampoo, so I just threw them in the dryer. Big mistake. Now I can barely button them, and I have to wear them to work because my other pants got a bleach stain on the knee. We're not supposed to wear jeans at the call center anyway, but Gary hasn't said anything yet. Probably because he's too busy worrying about his golf club tie clip. patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean... it definitely has. My work has slipped a lot lately. I missed some important notes in the CRM system the other day, and a call ended up escalating to management. I actually got written up for it. Which really sucks because I was hoping to move up to team lead eventually, and now I'm worried I completely blew my chance. 

Getting written up is the worst feeling. It's on this bright pink paper, too. Like, they actually use pink paper for the disciplinary forms. It's so embarrassing. Gary handed it to me in a folder, but everyone knows what it means when you get called into his office and come out with a manila folder. It's like being back in high school when you get sent to the principal's office and have to carry that little slip down the hallway. I hated high school. That's why I dropped out, honestly. I've been trying to study for my GED, but I've completely fallen behind on that, too. I'm just so exhausted all the time. And like I said, I'm avoiding all the people I used to hike with, so I'm just sitting around doing nothing, too tired to even look at a textbook. The GED prep book I bought is massive, too. It's like three inches thick. I tried reading the math section last week, and it was just a bunch of fractions and word problems about trains leaving stations at different times. Who even takes trains anymore? Unless you live in a big city with a subway, I guess. But yeah, avoiding all the trail stuff and the people I hiked with is definitely messing up my work and my studying.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't say I think I'm a bad person, really, but... I do keep thinking I was just so stupid and careless for being out there alone in the first place. Like, I should have known better. And now it just feels like if I let my guard down anywhere, something bad is going to happen. 

Being alone out there is kind of like when I try to study for my GED by myself at the coffee shop down the street. It's this little independent place, not a Starbucks, and they have these terrible wobbly tables. I tried shoving a napkin under one of the legs the other day, but it was one of those really cheap, thin napkins that just sort of disintegrates when you fold it. The barista there is this guy with a huge handlebar mustache, which I feel like is such an outdated look, you know? He always spells my name wrong on the cup even though I'm literally the only person in there most afternoons. He wrote 'Carl' last time. My name doesn't even sound like Carl. But yeah, I just feel like I was really dumb for being on that trail by myself, and now I'm just waiting for the next bad thing to happen if I'm not careful.

patient.answer:
Guilty? I don't know if guilt is the right word, but... I mean, most days I just feel scared and embarrassed right under the surface. Like everyone can tell I messed up out there and I'm not as tough as I used to act. 

Acting tough is so exhausting anyway. It's like my buddy Dave, he always acts like he's this huge tough guy because he drives a lifted truck. It's a Chevy Silverado, I think. Bright blue. He put these massive tires on it, and it's so high up you practically need a step stool to get in. I tore the seam on my good jacket trying to climb into the passenger seat once. It was this vintage windbreaker I found at a thrift store for like five bucks. The thrift store is right next to the bowling alley, which is weird because you always smell stale french fries when you're looking at the clothes. They have the best fries at that bowling alley, though. Crinkle cut. I don't know why, but crinkle cut just holds the ketchup better. But yeah, I just feel embarrassed all the time, like everyone knows I'm not actually tough at all.

I missed those important notes in the CRM, the call escalated, and I got that pink write-up slip from Gary. Which really still bothers me because I wanted to be a team lead. And I'm just so exhausted all the time that I've completely fallen behind on studying for my GED. I'm just avoiding everyone I used to hike with, so I sit around doing nothing. 

Sitting around is actually really bad for your posture, you know? I read this article online about how sitting too much is the new smoking. It messes up your lower back. My dad had terrible lower back problems. He used to wear this weird brace thing under his shirt that looked like a corset. He bought it off some infomercial late at night. Those infomercials are wild, they always have people struggling in black and white to do basic things, like pouring milk, and then suddenly in color they have this miracle product. I bought a slap-chop thing once because of an infomercial. It actually worked pretty well for onions, but it was a nightmare to clean. The blades would get stuck. But yeah, the memories and stuff are definitely causing problems with my job and my studying.
